title: YOU CALL HIM “LORD”—BUT WHAT IF JESUS ACTUALLY TOOK YOU AT YOUR WORD?
paragraphs:
YOU CALL HIM “LORD”—BUT WHAT IF JESUS ACTUALLY TOOK YOU AT YOUR WORD?
“Jesus Is Lord” may be the most familiar Christian confession on earth—and one of the most dangerous sentences to say without understanding what you have just confessed.
There is a sentence Christians sing.
We whisper it when life falls apart.
We shout it when prayers are answered.
We write it beneath photographs of sunsets, Bibles, baptisms, hospital recoveries, weddings, funerals, and testimonies.
Simple enough for a child to remember.
Powerful enough to rearrange an entire human life.
But somewhere between our lips and our living, something can go terribly wrong.
Because it is possible to call Jesus “Lord” while quietly reserving certain rooms of your life where He is not allowed to enter.
Your Sunday Christianity and your Monday decisions.
And suddenly the question becomes painfully personal:
What do you actually mean when you say, “Jesus is Lord”?
Because the earliest Christian confession was not merely, “Jesus helps me.”
It was not even merely, “Jesus saved me.”
hoti ean homologēsēs en tō stomati sou kyrion Iēsoun…
“If you confess with your mouth Jesus as Lord…”
The crucial words are κύριον Ἰησοῦν — kyrion Iēsoun — Jesus as Lord.

Paul joins that confession immediately to believing in your heart that God raised Jesus from the dead, promising salvation to the one who believes and confesses. Romans 10 does not present salvation as a reward for religious performance. It presents Christ as the One in whom righteousness is received by faith, and the confession of Jesus as Lord flows from that faith.
“Make Jesus Lord enough, obey well enough, clean yourself up enough, give enough, serve enough, and perhaps God will finally save you.”
The Gospel is far more shocking.
Christ bore judgment for His people.
You could not resurrect yourself spiritually any more than a corpse can perform CPR on itself.
It does not merely forgive rebels.
It does not merely cancel the record of sin.
It gives the sinner a new King.
That is where “Jesus is Lord” becomes uncomfortable.
Because everyone wants a Savior when the boat is sinking.
Far fewer people want a Lord when He begins telling them where the boat must go.
We love Jesus when He says, “Come to Me.”
But what happens when He says, “Follow Me”?
But what happens when forgiveness leads into repentance?
But what happens when grace begins dismantling the life we built without God?
We love the cross when Jesus is hanging on it.
But Jesus also told His followers to take up theirs.
That is the part modern Christianity can sometimes soften until discipleship becomes almost unrecognizable.
Jesus Himself asked a terrifyingly simple question:
“Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?”
Just Jesus confronting the distance between confession and obedience.
if My words never get the final word?
That question follows us into rooms nobody else sees.
Imagine the phone glowing against your face at 1:17 in the morning.
Nobody knows what you are looking at.
Nobody knows what conversation you deleted.
Nobody knows what fantasy you keep feeding.
Nobody knows what resentment you rehearse when you are alone.
Nobody knows how jealous you have become.
Nobody knows that you smile at church and quietly hate someone three rows away.
Nobody knows how exhausted you are from pretending.
Then, somewhere inside that darkness, comes the confession you have made a thousand times:
And suddenly it is no longer a slogan.
That is why repentance hurts before it heals.
Repentance forces us to stop negotiating with the God we claim to worship.
Some of us have spent years trying to make Jesus the constitutional monarch of our lives.
We want Jesus on the throne for photographs while we continue signing the laws.
But κύριος — kyrios — Lord is not decorative language.
And the New Testament pushes the confession even higher.
Paul writes of Christ in Philippians 2 that after His humiliation and obedience unto death, God highly exalted Him, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess:
And Paul says this confession is “to the glory of God the Father.”
Jesus is not campaigning for Lordship.
The question is not ultimately whether humanity will acknowledge Him.
Philippians says the day is coming when His Lordship will be universally confessed.
The question is whether you will bow before Him now in repentant faith and joyful surrender.
Because there is an enormous difference between surrendering to the King who saves you and finally facing the King you spent your life rejecting.
And perhaps that exposes something uncomfortable.
Maybe you do believe in Jesus.
But you have been fighting Him.
but you keep one hand wrapped around the thing He told you to release.
but there is someone you refuse even to begin forgiving.
You ask God to guide your future…
provided His answer resembles the future you already selected.
while secretly meaning, “as long as Your will does not cost me mine.”
And then grace interrupts the story.
Before you confessed the hidden thing, He knew.
Before anybody discovered your double life, He knew.
Before the night you became someone you promised yourself you would never become.
And still the Gospel came looking for sinners.
This is why Christianity is not the story of respectable people impressing God.
It is the story of a holy God rescuing guilty people through the crucified and risen Christ.
The man who had said he would die with Christ eventually insisted that he did not even know Him.
Imagine Peter after the rooster crowed.
Imagine remembering the sound of your own voice denying the One who loved you.
Imagine looking across that courtyard and realizing Jesus had been right about you.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
The kind of moment a human being would delete from his biography.
Yet Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
After the resurrection, Christ restored the disciple who had denied Him.
Not because Peter's betrayal did not matter.
But Peter's sin was not greater than Christ's grace.
Jesus did not call evil good.
He redeemed the man who had committed it.
That is the difference between cheap grace and biblical grace.
“It mattered enough for Me to bleed.”
Cheap grace makes peace with sin.
The Gospel makes peace with God through the blood of Christ—and then begins transforming the person who has been reconciled.
So when you confess, “Jesus is Lord,” you are not announcing that you have become perfect.
You are not saying you never struggle.
You are not saying temptation disappeared.
You are not saying you will never stumble again.
My struggle no longer gets to rename evil as good.
My culture does not have final authority.
My feelings do not have final authority.
My trauma does not have final authority.
My desires do not have final authority.
My political tribe does not have final authority.
My pastor does not have final authority.
Gospel Warrior does not have final authority.
And this is where some frightened believer needs to hear something equally important.
Do not turn Lordship into another ladder by which you attempt to climb into God's acceptance.
You cannot obey yourself into the cross.
The cross came down to you.

Ephesians 2:8–10 holds together what we are constantly tempted to tear apart: salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of our works so that no one can boast, yet those who are saved are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.
You do not obey Jesus so that His blood will finally become sufficient.
You obey because His blood is sufficient.
You do not repent to persuade God to become merciful.
You repent because in Christ you have encountered mercy.
You do not surrender so Jesus will finally love you.
You discover in the Gospel a love so costly that surrender becomes the only sane response.
This also means Christian obedience is not a commercial transaction.
You cannot share a Christian article and call that surrender.
You cannot donate enough money to erase one sin.
And perhaps that is exactly why genuine Christian generosity becomes beautiful.
Because when grace grips you, you stop asking only:
“What must I do to get something from God?”
“What has God entrusted to me that I can use for His glory?”
Even the little blue “share” button sitting underneath a Gospel message.
None of those things purchase heaven.
But all of them can become instruments placed in the hands of the King.
Maybe someone on your Facebook friends list has been silently drowning.
Maybe the person who jokes the loudest has been thinking about eternity.
Maybe somebody who has not entered a church in fifteen years will read an article because you shared it.
The friend you stopped talking to.
The believer who has slowly gone cold.
The skeptic who thinks Christians have nothing to offer except condemnation.
You do not know where a seed will land.
Send it privately to someone who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
If spreading biblical truth is one practical way you want to glorify God with the influence He has given you, then use that influence deliberately.
Maybe your comment becomes permission for another person to stop pretending.
There is no shame in needing prayer.
There is danger in becoming comfortable with hiding.
Not because saving a post makes you spiritual, but because tomorrow the emotions may fade.
And you may need to read again the question Jesus asked:
“Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?”
“Jesus, where am I calling You Lord but refusing Your authority?”
Maybe an obsession with being admired.
Maybe you have turned Christianity into content while your prayer life quietly died.
And when repentance makes you feel like running away from God…
Because repentance is not merely turning away from sin.
Christian repentance turns toward the Savior.
Toward the One whose hands still bear the testimony of what your forgiveness cost.
Toward the One who was crucified.
Toward the One who was buried.
Toward the One whom God raised from the dead.
Toward the One Romans tells us to confess as Lord.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because the scandal disappears from history.
The thief really was a criminal.
The prodigal really wasted what he had been given.
The Gospel does not require us to rewrite the past until we become the hero.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ entered the story.
And suddenly your worst chapter does not have the authority to write your final sentence.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build another personality cult.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to make people dependent upon a page.

But to keep placing Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, Gospel-centered discipleship, healing, repentance, restoration, and spiritual nourishment in front of people who desperately need Jesus.

If that mission has strengthened your walk with Christ, consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too.
But because Christian generosity can help Gospel-centered resources reach people who need them.
Your agreement does not make Him Lord.
Your obedience does not crown Him Lord.
Your surrender does not elect Him Lord.
The question is what you will do with the King who stands before you.
One day, Paul says, every knee will bow and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
And suddenly so much of what consumes us becomes painfully small.
The argument you needed to win.
The person whose approval controlled you.
The secret sin you thought you could never surrender.
The image you spent decades maintaining.
One day none of it will compete with the sight of Christ.
So why wait until eternity to acknowledge what is already true?
With the part of yourself you are terrified to surrender because you are afraid Jesus will destroy you if you finally give it to Him.
That is not the face of a Savior trying to destroy repentant sinners.
That is the King who died to redeem them.
Make restitution where biblical repentance requires it.
Seek accountability where you need it.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
Obey what Christ has clearly commanded.
Trust grace when shame tells you that your story is finished.
And never confuse struggling against sin with surrendering to it.
A believer may have nights when the battle feels unbearable.
But something inside the redeemed heart keeps returning to the throne:
Not the voices in my head.
That is the beginning of freedom.
“Jesus, be Lord of all of me.”
Not because a comment saves you.
But perhaps typing those words will become the moment you stop hiding from the question you already know He has been asking.
Because maybe the part of your life you are most afraid to place in His hands is the very place where grace is waiting to rewrite the story.
And when your shame whispers, “This chapter proves you are finished,” remember the nail-scarred King still holds the pen.
